pull.title: net: only monitor select exceptions while connecting
pull.body:
Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
>
> This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

Fix this by only adding a socket to the `select()` exception set while waiting for a non-blocking `connect()` to complete. Windows needs that to detect a failed connection. Established connections no longer monitor the exception set on any platform. This approach was suggested by theuni in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716#issuecomment-6931290348 and replaces the earlier version of this PR, which ignored the exception set outside Windows and disconnected on it on Windows.

We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

The PR makes one additional change for clarity: if `errorSet` is reported for a socket we did not request to read from, disconnect directly instead of first attempting a send that would fail (emits a different log message). `if (recvSet || errorSet)` is left as is. Since `select()` no longer reports errors for established connections, this only applies to `poll()`.

Test coverage is introduced in `p2p_socket_errors.py`.

Finally the same early error check is applied to HTTP, with urgent data coverage in `interface_http.py`.

events.body:
I dropped the comment-only commit.

Added two commits based on @vasild's feedback.

Also added and expanded @pinheadmz's tests.

Finally, I added the http fix at the end. It should be simple to review since it's the same approach.

I also tested on Windows native.

> We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

I believe it's possible to construct an oob urgent ptr for data which will never be sent and which will then never be received but will still trigger the exception set. Setting SO_OOBINLINE thus can't ultimately clear the select() exception because no data is actually inline to read. On the BSDs I examined (and therefore likely OS/X) this will still generate an exception so the current select() call will return immediately again. As noted elsewhere, this doesn't technically prevent eventual node progress.

fwiw, I strongly suggest that oob data be considered an error condition based on this. There is nowhere for UNIX-y OSes which an oob byte will ever be generated by a valid p2p peer, and thus it'll only ever be generated in this context — therefore disconnection is a logical and completely fair result. I personally think at this point it's worth a ban.

(Uh, just to be clear, at the very least I think we should delete the exceptfds from the select() call entirely, so strong ACK for this approach.)

> I strongly suggest that oob data be considered an error condition based on this

I agree that if there was a `DISCONNECT_ON_OOB` flag, we should set it. But we can't directly detect if such data was present. All we can know is that `errorSet` was triggered, which could be for unrelated OS reasons. That could cause us to disconnect a well behaved peer.

That's why this PR simply ignores the exception set (outside Windows), instead of trying to handle it. It might be possible with poll(), but that would be better for a followup.

@midnightmagic agreed.

Imo we should just always disconnect when an exception is set, or when oob/prio are found. I don't see any need for platform-specific behavior here. I'd rather go with: https://github.com/theuni/bitcoin/commits/net-oob-error/

That branch unifies the select/poll behaviors, and causes a disconnect (on all platforms) if any of those conditions are true.

It differs from what's here in that it turns `POLLHUP` into a read event as it should be, rather than an error. That simplifies things significantly, as it allows draining to happen naturally, and it means that the exception set is truly only comprised of exceptions.

If receiving is off (meaning that we have data to send) and we receive a SIGHUP, we'll disconnect on the next send.

It fixes up the tests to show that OOB data always causes a disconnect.

Rebased after #36744.

@theuni wrote:

> Imo we should just always disconnect when an exception is set

So you're not worried about the operating system triggering this set for reasons that have nothing to do with OOB data?

> That branch unifies the select/poll behaviors, and causes a disconnect (on all platforms) if any of those conditions are true.

Since that's a completely different approach from this PR, it seems better to open it as a separate (and alternative) PR.

Ok, I retract the above. After experimenting for the last few days, nothing really works here to align the two behaviors without logical hacks.

I really dislike the platform-specific hacks here, but I agree that they're a necessary evil as long as we're supporting `select` and `poll`. I'll drop the suggestion to use my branch and review what's here for correctness.

Sorry to throw yet another wrench in this, but when trying to tease apart the uses and platform differences for the select error set, it occurred to me that all of the hacks have to do with the fact that we have a single obscure use-case for that set, and in all other cases it's harmful. Rather than trying to isolate the platforms that require that use-case, why not isolate the use-case instead?

Please see here: https://github.com/theuni/bitcoin/commit/f8fbc168bbe0995d498a1ee594515869a78d4361 for a change that splits out the connection failure case. That allows us to completely ignore the select error set in all other cases where it'd be considered harmful. Imo that's much cleaner because it requires a single opt-in where needed, rather than opt-outs sprinkled all around.

With that change, I don't think the early `if (errorSet && !recvSet)` disconnects are needed at all, but could (and probably should) be added for belt-and-suspenders.

@Sjors @darosior mind taking a look?

net: only use the select error set while connecting

Windows uses the select() error set to report a failed non-blocking
connect(). Add ConnErrorEventFlag, which ConnectToSocket() passes to
Sock::Wait() to opt in to the error set while connecting. This is safe
on all platforms, as any error condition is worth waking for there.

All other uses of select() now leave the error set empty. With
select(), sockets waited on without the flag no longer wake up for or
report exceptional conditions, such as TCP urgent data on an
established connection. No behavior change with poll().

Co-authored-by: Cory Fields <cory-nospam-@coryfields.com>

events.body:
@theuni to put it into my own words, IIUC:

There's two phases to a connection, phase 1 establishes it `ConnectToSocket` and phase 2 maintains it after (in `GenerateWaitSockets`, etc). Your proposal makes it so that in phase 2 nothing watches `errorSet`, while in phase 1 it's now watched on all platforms. A follow-up could narrow phase 1 to just Windows as belt-and-suspenders.

This makes sense, and I adopted it.

On ancient versions of Windows it was unsafe to ignore `errorSet`, and it had to be drained to prevent memory exhaustion. See https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/tcpm/55ecR94wP1NkrL5cuPj0PWtTIXc/

The following checks for this:  https://gist.github.com/Sjors/9582259267a038e06c7f0730356416de 

I tested on a physical Windows 11 Home 26H2 machine. Connections reset after 17 urgent bytes. I also tested Windows Server 2022 on a Github CI runner: https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/actions/runs/44390882699/job/135107875034

The latter should roughly match Windows 10 in this regard, which is the oldest version we support. So this is no longer a concern in theory, but it doesn't hurt to actually try if you can find such a machine.

BSD is probably also worth testing, cc @vasild.

Approach ACK, thanks for the update.

See my comment about keeping the `(recvSet || errorSet)` check as-is.

Other than that, looks good to me.

events.body:
This PR has changed multiple times, and considerably grown, since it was opened. And it's also losing momentum, whereas it's currently the main PR for an important fix. So i think it's worth taking a step back and asking what it's trying to achieve.

I think the initial goal was to get a minimal fix in, because a proper cleanup of this logic like #36761 would be riskier to backport. But now this PR adds as much code as [switching to poll entirely](https://github.com/darosior/bitcoin/compare/2610_ditch_select~6..2610_ditch_select) (and removes 10 times less).

It's not exactly trivial code either: we introduce new flags to Sock, leak the connection stage down to the socket wait logic to only register the exception set at this point, have some callers (but not all!) now disconnect on errors.. That's a bunch of behaviour changes not strictly necessary to fix the bug, that i would be hesitant to backport (i.e. ship with much less testing --especially if we deem the bug important enough to cut minor releases as soon as the fix is ready).

On top of that, this PR adds a whole bunch of functional tests that seem pretty brittle to me, since they rely on kernel settings that may differ between machines, or break when we update CI (that's the reason why i did not push similar tests i had performed locally to #36688). It's also not clear to me how useful they are, as they wouldn't even catch the bug this PR set out to fix in the first place (following my review comment below i tested this by cherry-picking your tests on master and running them on a Windows VM).

Why not go back to the simple approach of simply always disconnecting when a wait returns an `ErrorEvent`? It's short, easy to reason about and safer to backport.

Sure, it preserves the behaviour difference between platforms using select() and those using poll(). That can be cleaned up later, in a more involved change we don't intend to backport, since this is a pre-existing issue.

I'm thinking about something like this https://github.com/darosior/bitcoin/commit/97666aa7a6230641af7e00e372ec1dbd88436c92.

> > I strongly suggest that oob data be considered an error condition based on this
> 
> I agree that if there was a `DISCONNECT_ON_OOB` flag, we should set it. But we can't directly detect if such data was present. All we can know is that `errorSet` was triggered, which could be for unrelated OS reasons. That could cause us to disconnect a well behaved peer.
> 
> That's why this PR simply ignores the exception set (outside Windows), instead of trying to handle it. It might be possible with poll(), but that would be better for a followup.

Minor context: On many OSes (mostly BSD-derived) I believe there is only a single trigger for the exceptfd set in a select() call for a normal TCP socket and that's OOB data. The reason to consider OOB data now almost certainly hostile incoming data in all cases is because the codebase's current (?) behaviour makes it so the only reasonable interpretation is a hostile action — i.e. there is no well-behaving peer which will ever generate OOB data and send it to us.

If the codebase ignores it in a way where someone sending it means nothing — yes absolutely that will solve the problem in the least and most minimally-invasive fashion, and people like myself will just run our own detection patch independently. I agree with you in that if we're immune to it in the first place, detecting it above that is just special-case pointlessness. My only concern really is making sure the .. uh error condition isn't possible anymore. So, yeah you're right.

Elsewise if we retain the ability to detect OOB data, a noisy log entry and a disconnect would be welcome to folks like myself but certainly not necessary. I really don't have a particular dog in this race either way, and I'll just be grateful when the error condition gets fixed.

@darosior would it make sense to merge this and backport your simpler version?

If you do want to go for a different approach, it's better if you or someone else  (possibly me) opens a PR for that, rather than changing this PR back and forth.

The tests were added because reviewers suggested them. You're the first to push back on them. They help illustrate what this PR changes and what stays the same. For the master branch I think they're fine, and if they turn out difficult to maintain they can just be dropped.

> especially if we deem the bug important enough to cut minor releases as soon as the fix is ready

I don't think it is based on my current understanding. I would rather see the backport properly tested, and then it can be shipped along with whatever more urgent backport fix comes next.

I don't think it makes sense to backport something different than what gets merged on master. The vast majority of our testing comes from development, which happens on master. Release candidates barely receive any testing. Backporting something other than what gets merged in master boils down to releasing code that will only have been tested / ran by whomever looks at the backport PRs (which usually get less attention than regular PRs). At that point i'd rather we don't backport anything.

I didn't want to step on your toes, and figured it would be better that we concentrate attention on a single PR to fix this bug. But i also agree with changing this PR back and forth, and if you'd rather i open a different approach, and reviewers can judge which they prefer, i am happy to do that.

Why insist on committing to master tests that do not even catch the bug you are fixing, but still may introduce flakiness because they rely on low level kernel parameters which may change across time and machines? That just does not make any sense to me.

I agree it is not necessary to rush a minor release for this. Having it backported in the branch, ready to be released, would be good though: it means that we can make binaries available within a couple days if people are encountering the issue in the wild.

I plan to drop the http commit to make it easier to backport, given that 30.x and 31.x still use Libevent. I'll open a follow-up with that (if and) after this is merged.

> On top of that, this PR adds a whole bunch of functional tests that seem pretty brittle to me

I tested backports down to 29.x, which indeed reveals problems. I'm going to try to make the test more robust, and otherwise drop it and instead add it to a gist that reviewers can use (like the windows stress test).

> tests that do not even catch the bug you are fixing

You said it was brittle, not that it didn't work. Obviously I don't want to include tests that don't work.
Opened my suggested alternative as https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36953.

> It's not exactly trivial code either: we introduce new flags to Sock, leak the connection stage down to the socket wait logic to only register the exception set at this point, have some callers (but not all!) now disconnect on errors.. That's a bunch of behaviour changes not strictly necessary to fix the bug, that i would be hesitant to backport (i.e. ship with much less testing --especially if we deem the bug important enough to cut minor releases as soon as the fix is ready).

I disagree with this framing. Yes, it was a winding road to get here, but the changes are straightforward:
- Disconnect if we didn't request a read, but we get a hup/error event. This prevents us from reading when we shouldn't because we're paused. Afaik this would be safe to add by itself.
- Registering for errors when using `select` is harmful in all but one case (detecting connection failures), and in that one it is required. Require callers to opt-in if they require this failure. For `poll`, this is a noop. This has the effect of disabling select "errors" that weren't really errors.

Otherwise, things stay the same. Draining for `poll`/`select` happens as before, but we avoid the harmful non-error "errors".  We could add a few harmless `#if[n]def USE_POLL` in the higher layers to demonstrate where the changes have effects if that would help?

As I mentioned above, the less hackish way of doing this would be to introduce a `WaitForNewConnection()` which would be straightforward as the only way to register for an error event when using `select`. I proposed the more hackish event flag here instead to avoid having to change the `Sock` class and its derivatives, and the tests/fuzzers to go with it. I don't think we can have it all here.. either a quick hack that is small and targeted and backportable, or a more correct fix that's more invasive.

> 
> On top of that, this PR adds a whole bunch of functional tests that seem pretty brittle to me, since they rely on kernel settings that may differ between machines, or break when we update CI (that's the reason why i did not push similar tests i had performed locally to #36688). It's also not clear to me how useful they are, as they wouldn't even catch the bug this PR set out to fix in the first place (following my review comment below i tested this by cherry-picking your tests on master and running them on a Windows VM).
> 

I'll admit I don't love the tests for this either. I'm not sure what to add here.

> Why not go back to the simple approach of simply always disconnecting when a wait returns an `ErrorEvent`? It's short, easy to reason about and safer to backport.
> 

IIRC my tests showed this was a behavioral change on Linux as we no longer do any socket draining once that error is received. We've had some discussions offline about the importance of that... I'm willing to concede that it might not matter in the end, but I'd be nervous to just assume it's fine and backport it. So to me, that's actually harder to reason about.

@theuni i agree with your concern but there is no behaviour change on Linux for a clean connection close. My approach leads to an earlier disconnect only in case a connection is reset. I'm investigating now how "normal" such connection resets are, and whether we do actually handle them properly today.

> 1) discourages applications from sending urgent data

The RFC says:

> Even though applications SHOULD NOT employ the urgent mechanism

This isn't about a misbehaving sender, but rather about application design (both sides).

> This does not follow

I'm not sure what exactly "this" refers to. It's true that the RFC does not forbid applications from setting `SO_OOBINLINE` if they don't "employ urgent indications".

I do think it's good to document that we don't "employ urgent indications". The absence of the setting implies it, but an actual code comment is more clear.

In any case, I'll drop the comment commit.

> Should the below `if (recvSet || errorSet)` be revised as well?

I added a commit to check `errorSet` separately and earlier, for `poll()`.

I spent some time trying to understand if that's a behavior change, but AFAIK it just emits a different log message. I added a test to demonstrate that.

comments.body:
I experimented with removing `select()` entirely on top of this changeset, and ended up needing a little change here. Rather than `recvSet`, what we really want to test (as your comment states) is `recvReq`, where
```c++
bool recvReq = it->second.requested & Sock::RecvEvent;
```

I don't think it matters here, but in order to support poll in a cross-platform way, the exact condition we want to test is "did we see an error when we didn't request a receive event", which is slightly different than "did we see an error when we didn't SEE a receive event" as we have here.

This matters for platforms (Windows) which raise only `POLLERR | POLLHUP` for disconnections, even when `POLLIN` was requested.

Again.. it shouldn't matter here. Just pointing it out for the future.

According to the `poll` Linux manpage, we may receive a lone `POLLHUP` (without `POLLIN` or `POLLERR`) when the socket has been drained and the next recv would close it. I think if we skip the `|| errorSet` here, we could end up waking for the error (`POLLHUP`) event, and never doing anything with it. Then we're back to the tight loop.

Since `select` is a no-op here now, I don't see the harm in leaving this as `if (recvSet || errorSet)` ?

Here's the output of the Linux manpage example. It's a file descriptor rather than a socket, it's possible that the behavior is different.

```bash
 $ ./poll myfifo
Opened "myfifo" on fd 3
About to poll()
Ready: 1
  fd=3; events: POLLIN POLLHUP
    read 4 bytes: foo

About to poll()
Ready: 1
  fd=3; events: POLLHUP
    closing fd 3
All file descriptors closed; bye
```

The concept of `recvRequested` makes a lot of sense, so I added this and used it for the early disconnect.

67bdc2d3b5c62dd4d8cf0eb757b78fcf0d5b56b3 -> 8b8a2f49267daa6a3f9d85d9cb511bd7c286e52a

Also applied to http in 05084e7879140aaf7c9b77e372ebc828f98e3153.

> I think if we skip the `|| errorSet` here

The poll code in `WaitMany` sets `errorSet` if it gets POLLHUP. The `if (errorSet && !recvSet)` check above disconnects, so we don't get here. 

I still dropped this change: 67bdc2d3b5c62dd4d8cf0eb757b78fcf0d5b56b3 -> 8b8a2f49267daa6a3f9d85d9cb511bd7c286e52a

Given that `SocketHandlerConnected()` only handles established connections:
- with `select()`, `errorSet` is never set, so `recvSet || errorSet` is just `recvSet`
- with `poll()`, a lone `POLLHUP` or `POLLERR` gives `errorSet && !recvSet`, which the early disconnect above already handles

Just keeping the low half reserved for Events and the high for Flags. I can't imagine it matters in any real way... `1 << 3` is fine if you prefer it.

After all, this is just a hack to keep the diff small as opposed to adding the more straightforward `WaitForNewConnection()` function.
